items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover that a clogged filter could revolutionize oil refining
items.content_html: Scientists have developed a remarkable new membrane that separates crude oil at room temperature, using the oil itself to create microscopic filtration channels. The breakthrough could cut refining energy consumption by nearly 32%, carbon emissions by almost 38%, and operating costs by 36%, potentially transforming one of the world's most energy-intensive industries.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] A clever molecular trick unlocks previously impossible properties in glass
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered how to reprogram the internal structure of glass using a special molecule that rearranges chemical bonds while lowering the melting temperature. The breakthrough could unlock entirely new glass materials with precisely controlled magnetic and optical properties, opening possibilities for advanced electronics, sensors, and other technologies.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss
items.content_html: Scientists have uncovered a surprising link between Alzheimer’s-related protein buildup, disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, and fading memory. The findings suggest that hidden changes in how the brain processes memories overnight may contribute to age-related memory loss long before Alzheimer’s symptoms appear.

items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Scientists have discovered that a simple mechanical squeeze can dramatically alter the magnetic properties and electrical behavior of exotic materials called altermagnets. The surprising breakthrough could open the door to faster, more energy-efficient electronics and new technologies for quantum computing.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] MIT scientists break a 20-year rule and unlock never-before-seen crystal structures
items.content_html: MIT scientists have challenged two decades of conventional thinking by discovering that flexible molecular connections, rather than rigid ones, can unlock entirely new ways to arrange nanoparticles. The breakthrough could lead to a new generation of designer materials with unusual properties and applications in electronics, medicine, and energy.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope
items.content_html: NASA is exploring a daring plan to save the legendary Hubble Space Telescope from its eventual fiery plunge into Earth's atmosphere. After more than 35 years of groundbreaking discoveries, Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without intervention, it could fall back to Earth as early as 2033 or 2034. To keep the iconic observatory operating, NASA is asking private space companies to propose innovative ways to boost Hubble into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it when its mission finally ends.

items.title: [science.org] JWST image-processing method boosts exoplanet sensitivity up to 15-fold
items.content_html: Astronomers have developed a physics-based method to remove residual starlight from James Webb Space Telescope images, improving sensitivity to faint planets by two to 15 times and revealing the known giant exoplanet 51 Eridani b at a wavelength where earlier processing failed. The method, called Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets, or FLIP, models the telescope’s optics and adjusts for small changes that make conventional reference-star images imperfect matches. The method works with existing observations without changes to telescope hardware. The team is now reprocessing the hundreds of coronagraphic images JWST has collected to look for additional planets. Researchers say the approach could ease strict stability requirements for future observatories, but further work is needed to reduce computing costs and test it on larger data sets.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] SLAC scientists find conclusive proof of a mysterious third type of magnetism
items.content_html: For nearly 90 years, scientists believed magnetism fell into just two categories, but researchers have now confirmed a remarkable third type called altermagnetism. Using specialized X-rays, they uncovered a unique magnetic signature that proves these materials behave differently from conventional magnets. Altermagnets combine stability with the ability to efficiently carry information, potentially overcoming major limitations in today's electronics. The discovery could lead to faster computers, more efficient data centers, and breakthroughs in quantum technology.

items.title: 🔓 [WIRED] Chernobyl’s Dogs May Be Evolving, but Scientists Don’t Know Why
items.content_html: A new study found evidence of natural selection in the dogs of Chernobyl, but it’s still unclear what drove these genetic differences and what evolutionary advantages they may provide.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists trick cancer cells into making the drugs that kill them
items.content_html: Scientists have developed a promising new cancer-fighting strategy that uses carbon monoxide naturally produced by tumor cells to manufacture powerful drugs inside the cancer cells themselves. Early laboratory experiments suggest the technique could selectively attack cancer while sparing healthy cells, potentially paving the way for safer chemotherapy alternatives.

items.title: [discovermagazine.com] NASA engineers extend Voyager 1 operations before one-light-day mark
items.content_html: NASA engineers have kept Voyager 1’s remaining science instruments running longer by replacing three power-hungry heating devices with lower-power alternatives, as the probe approaches a distance of one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026. Engineers completed the change, called the “Big Bang,” in September to delay another instrument shutdown that otherwise could have come by summer 2027. The probe, launched in 1977, briefly stopped communicating after scheduled communication attempts on Oct. 18 and 19; its signal returned on Oct. 20. Engineers found that a set of thrusters had gone offline and the spacecraft had automatically switched to its backup, but NASA’s Voyager team has not identified the cause of the interruption. On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be about 16.09 billion miles from Earth, with a 24-hour one-way signal delay and a 48-hour round trip.

items.title: [sci.news] CERN experiment reports first evidence of ultra-rare beauty meson decay
items.content_html: The LHCb collaboration at CERN reported the first evidence of a neutral beauty meson (B⁰) decaying into two muons, a process predicted to occur about once in every 10 billion such particles. Combining the new result with earlier LHCb data gave the signal a statistical significance of 3.2 standard deviations—enough to count as evidence, but below the five-standard-deviation threshold for a discovery. The measured rate is consistent with the Standard Model, the leading theory of particle physics. Rare decays can be sensitive to effects from particles that are not produced directly in collisions. Researchers plan to continue collecting data into the early 2030s to refine the measurement; a further detector upgrade is also planned.

items.title: [Nautilus] Could One Brain Region Be Tied to Feeling Sick All Over?
items.content_html:
When you break your foot, the pain is mostly confined to your foot. When you get the flu or another systemic infection, your entire being aches: Lethargy creeps into your limbs, your appetite vanishes, your temperature jags between scorching and chilled to the bone, and you just want to pull the covers over your head.

This kind of overpowering mind-body malaise is known as “sickness syndrome,” and it’s considered a distinct physiological and emotional state. Scientists believe sickness syndrome helps the body prepare to fight infections, but they don’t fully understand what is happening in the brain when this storm cloud descends.

Read more: “How to Unlearn a Disease”

items.title: [ScienceDaily] The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
items.content_html: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism could help explain why people with anxiety or PTSD sometimes experience intense fear in completely safe situations.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] The Amazon’s canary in the coalmine: what a tropical fish can tell us about climate upheaval
items.content_html:
Scientist Adalberto Luis Val’s pioneering research on the tambaqui fish is revealing the effect of climate disruption in Brazil, with global implications for biodiversity and food security

As a boy in rural São Paulo, Adalberto Luis Val used to stare into the lake where his father took him fishing and wonder how all those creatures swimming below stayed alive. One day, he netted a few, put them in a jar, and brought them home to observe. The next morning, they were all dead. Val was devastated but intrigued.

“I needed to know how fish are able to live,” he says.

items.title: [Reason] Identifying Plasma Proteins Associated with Mortality Risk and Biological Age
items.content_html: Researchers here report on the results of screening a few thousand proteins found in blood plasma for those where levels correlate with (a) risk of mortality and (b) organ-specific biological age, using a consensus approach to determining those biological age measures from proteomic data. The usual caveats apply regarding whether or not such an aging clock is actually measuring biological age, or would still produce decent data if an anti-aging intervention were involved, but gathering more data on the performance of such clocks is nonetheless a potentially useful activity. items.title: [ScienceDaily] All 5 genetic “letters” of DNA and RNA discovered in a 4.5-billion-year-old asteroid
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered all five essential nucleobases used in DNA and RNA in pristine samples from asteroid Ryugu, revealing that key ingredients for life existed in space billions of years ago. The remarkable finding adds to growing evidence from other asteroids and meteorites that these molecules were widespread throughout the early Solar System.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half
items.content_html: A surprising discovery suggests that rejuvenating the liver could help protect against Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease. USC researchers found that an experimental drug restored aging liver cells in rats, cutting levels of an Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half and bringing bad cholesterol down to youthful levels. The treatment also revived a previously unknown communication system that helps liver cells remove harmful substances from the bloodstream.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] IceCube detects ghost particles with 10 billion times the energy of solar neutrinos
items.content_html: Mysterious particles called neutrinos constantly stream through our bodies, and scientists are now detecting incredibly powerful versions arriving from distant cosmic sources using a massive observatory buried in Antarctic ice. These elusive “ghost particles” could hold extraordinary clues about the Big Bang, extreme cosmic events, and some of the universe’s greatest mysteries.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover that some “unhealthy” diets can boost cancer immunotherapy in mice
items.content_html: In a surprising discovery, scientists found that certain diets associated with obesity can make cancer immunotherapy more effective in mice, challenging traditional assumptions about diet and cancer treatment. The findings suggest that the secret may lie in how food interacts with gut bacteria to strengthen the immune system's response to cancer.

items.title: [New Atlas] Harvard smartphone app guides the blind faster, with fewer collisions
items.content_html:
If you have standard human vision (even if assisted by glasses), chances are you’re adept at finding things, people, and paths to them. But if you have impaired vision, or none at all, countless tasks that are simple for fully sighted people become difficult, dangerous, or even impossible. Fortunately, plenty of new high-tech tools offer assistance, including robot guide dogs, a cane-bot (looking a bit like a small R2D2 with giant wheels), multiple types of smart glasses with descriptive audio, and even a haptic vest for blind dogs.
